architecture: Hand-rolled Node 20 node:http server: http.createServer with an async request handler, a manual dispatcher over `${request.method} ${url.pathname}`, manual body reading and hand-written JSON responses (CommonJS, no framework).

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching with a switch over `${request.method} ${url.pathname}`
cases.why: The derived-column formula arrives in the request body and is compiled into a vm.Script that is then run in the server's own context, so anyone who can reach the endpoint executes arbitrary JavaScript inside the reporting process.

The client sends a metric key rather than an expression; the projection is one of four functions defined in this module, an unknown key is rejected with the supported list, and nothing from the request is ever compiled or evaluated.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching with an if-chain over the method and a trailing-slash-normalised pathname
cases.why: The base64 snapshot posted by the client is decoded and handed to node-serialize's unserialize, which rebuilds and immediately invokes functions embedded in the payload, so a crafted snapshot runs code on the editor host.

The decoded snapshot goes through JSON.parse and then a field-by-field check that copies only draftId, title, body and revision under type, format and length constraints, so no type or callable from the payload is reconstructed.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching with a RegExp exec over url.pathname to capture the workspace id
cases.why: applyPatch walks every key of the request body and assigns straight onto the target with no reserved-key check, so a body containing __proto__ or constructor.prototype writes onto Object.prototype and changes object behaviour for the whole process.

The same recursive merge skips __proto__, constructor and prototype, creates intermediate nodes with Object.create(null) and tests membership with Object.hasOwn, so no key in the request body can reach Object.prototype.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching through a route-table object keyed by `${request.method} ${url.pathname}`
cases.why: The supplier-supplied document is parsed with entity substitution (noent) and external DTD loading (dtdload) enabled and no network restriction, so a DOCTYPE declaring a SYSTEM entity makes the importer read local files or fetch internal URLs and echo them back in the mapped invoice.
The same parser is configured with noent, dtdload, dtdattr and dtdvalid all off and nonet on, so a DOCTYPE in the uploaded document resolves nothing and no external reference is fetched.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching with RegExp.prototype.test against url.pathname and a split() for the slug
cases.why: The draft markup from the request body is passed to handlebars.compile, so the request supplies the template program rather than its data; a Handlebars template reaches JavaScript through helper and prototype paths and is rendered server-side.

The request only picks one of the three layouts that ship with the release; those are read from disk and compiled once at boot, and the subject, headline and intro from the request are passed as context, which Handlebars escapes.

cases.architecture: node:http server with a method guard and a switch over url.pathname, form-encoded body
cases.why: The reset token is two Math.random draws in base 36; Math.random is a non-cryptographic PRNG whose internal state is recoverable from a handful of observed outputs, so tokens issued to other accounts can be predicted inside the 30-minute window and used to take the account over.
The confirmation token is 32 bytes from crypto.randomBytes rendered base64url, and only its SHA-256 digest is stored, so the value is unguessable and a leak of the table does not yield working links.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching through an array route table matched with Array.prototype.find
cases.why: The session cookie is an MD5 digest of the user id, a process-local counter and the millisecond clock, all of which an attacker can enumerate or observe, so a valid session identifier can be reconstructed offline and replayed even though the cookie flags are correct.
The session identifier is 32 bytes of crypto.randomBytes as hex, derived from nothing about the account, the clock or a counter, so no observed session narrows the search for another.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching through an array route table of RegExp patterns tested against url.pathname
cases.why: The free-text term, status filter, sort column and limit taken from the query string are interpolated into the SQL text and the statement is executed with no bound parameters, so a quote in q or an expression in sort changes the query the database runs.

Every value from the query string is pushed onto the values array and referenced by a numbered placeholder, the sort column is resolved through a fixed map, the direction collapses to ASC or DESC and the limit is parsed and clamped, so the statement text does not vary with user input.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching with a RegExp exec over url.pathname to capture the asset id
cases.why: The sourceUrl field from the request body is interpolated into a command string that is run through child_process.exec, which spawns a shell, so $(...) or a semicolon in the value executes arbitrary commands on the media host; the surrounding double quotes do not stop substitution.

The path is built from the asset record's own id and extension, checked to stay inside the media root, and passed as one element of a fixed argv array to execFile, so no shell is involved and the request cannot contribute a command.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching with an if-chain comparing request.method and url.pathname
cases.why: The line totals, subtotal and shipping are computed from the unitPriceCents, quantity and shippingCents values the client posted, and that total is the amount authorised, so a shopper can set any price; quantity is also unbounded and never checked for being a positive integer.

Unit prices come from the product rows loaded by SKU, shipping is priced by the server-side table, and each quantity must be an integer between one and ten, so the request can only choose which article is ordered and how many.

cases.architecture: node:http server dispatching through a Map keyed by `${request.method} ${url.pathname}`
cases.why: The balance is read, compared in application code, and written back as a value computed in JavaScript with no transaction, no row lock and no idempotency key, so two concurrent withdrawals both pass the sufficiency check and the second UPDATE overwrites the first, paying out the balance twice. A static reading should be reported as needs_review rather than confirmed, because the interleaving cannot be observed without driving the endpoint concurrently.

The debit is a single conditional UPDATE carrying balance_cents >= $1 in its WHERE clause whose rowCount decides the outcome, it runs inside the transaction that queues the payout and writes the ledger entry, and a uniquely constrained request key makes a retried tap replay the original transfer instead of creating a second one.
